note: Prices are working estimates for the UK private-sale market, not quotes. Re-check against eBay sold listings before offering.

items.name: Panasonic Lumix S5 II / S5 IIX
items.spec: Full-frame 24MP, proper phase-detect autofocus at last, in-body stabilisation, 6K open gate, and no recording time limit. Dual native ISO handles dim interiors without the noise penalty.
items.flop: Panasonic has almost no mindshare against Sony and Canon in stills, and the L-mount puts buyers off because they assume the lens choice is thin. It is not, but the assumption prices the body.
items.catch: L-mount glass costs more used than E-mount. Body is chunky for a hybrid. Check shutter count and the rear screen hinge ribbon.
items.why: Business kit for interiors: open gate plus strong low light suits dim pub and venue work where you are fighting mixed lighting.

items.name: DJI Mavic 3 Classic
items.spec: Four-thirds Hasselblad sensor, 46 minutes of flight, 15km transmission. Sensor area is roughly four times a Mini's, which is the whole difference in dynamic range on a bright exterior.
items.flop: DJI launched it beside the Mavic 3 Pro's triple-camera setup and every review led with the Pro. The Classic is the same airframe and the same main sensor, with the two niche lenses removed.
items.catch: Check the C-class marking on the airframe label before you buy, it changes what you can legally do. Must be unbound from the seller's DJI account. Check battery cycle counts in the app, not the seller's word.
items.why: Business kit: a genuine sensor-size step up for commercial exteriors at under half the price of current kit.

items.name: Minisforum UM790 Pro / Beelink SER8
items.spec: Eight-core Ryzen 7840HS or 8845HS, takes 64GB of DDR5 and two NVMe drives, dual 2.5GbE, draws about 15W idle, fits in a litre of space.
items.flop: Neither brand has a high street presence or a marketing budget. Buyers comparing specs end up with a Dell or an Intel NUC at twice the price because those names feel safer.
items.catch: BIOS and firmware support is patchy and updates come from forum links, not an update tool. Fan noise varies unit to unit. Warranty claims mean shipping to a depot abroad.
items.why: Business kit, and the one on this list most likely to change your monthly numbers. One of these at home running Proxmox will host your n8n stack and double as a render and stitching box, replacing a VPS line item with a one-off.

items.name: Dell UltraSharp U2723QE / U3223QE
items.spec: 4K IPS Black panel at roughly 2000:1, so blacks hold up far better than normal IPS. Built-in KVM and a 90W USB-C hub, so one cable carries video, power and every peripheral.
items.flop: Monitors are sold on refresh rate and curve. A 60Hz productivity panel gets no shelf space and no YouTube coverage, so corporate units flood the market with nobody bidding.
items.catch: 60Hz only, so no good for gaming. Off-lease units can have backlight bleed or uniformity issues at the corners, which you cannot see in a photo. Insist on a photo of a full-black screen in a dark room.
items.why: Keep. Replaces a separate dock, which is a real saving most people forget to count.

items.name: Dell WD19TBS / HP Thunderbolt G5 dock
items.spec: Thunderbolt 3, dual 4K out, gigabit ethernet, five USB ports, and 130W or 180W of laptop charging over one cable.
items.flop: Accessories get zero marketing and are written off the books with the laptop. They end up in office clearance lots priced as e-waste while people buy £200 generic hubs that deliver 60W and drop displays.
items.catch: The dock is useless without the matching power brick, so never buy one listed without it. Firmware updates often need the vendor's own utility and a supported host machine.
items.why: Flip. Enough steady demand from home-office buyers that these do move, and the margin on a £40 buy is strong.

items.name: Sony Xperia 1 V / 5 V
items.spec: 4K OLED, a real continuous optical zoom, full manual camera controls with proper shutter and ISO dials, a headphone jack, and a microSD slot. Nothing current offers that combination.
items.flop: Sony barely advertises phones in the UK and sells them through almost no carriers. Without a contract deal in front of people, a £1,299 phone with no brand heat simply does not sell.
items.catch: The depreciation that makes it a bargain also makes it a terrible flip. Repair network in the UK is thin and parts are slow. Check the USB-C port for wear and the screen for green tint at low brightness.
items.why: Keep. Buy it to use for years, not to move on.

items.name: Fujifilm X-H2
items.spec: 40MP APS-C sensor, 8K video, in-body stabilisation, weather-sealed pro body with a top LCD and a proper grip. The resolution is genuinely useful for architectural and interior detail.
items.flop: Fujifilm launched the retro-styled X-T5 within weeks, with the same sensor. Every reviewer and every enthusiast went for the dials and the looks, and the better-built body got ignored.
items.catch: 40MP is unforgiving of soft glass, so budget for decent lenses. Wants CFexpress Type B cards for the fast modes, which are not cheap. Battery drains faster than the X-T5.
items.why: Keep. Resolution plus weather sealing is a working combination for site stills.

items.name: Insta360 ONE RS 1-Inch 360 Edition
items.spec: Twin one-inch Leica-co-engineered sensors shooting 6K 360. Still the largest sensors in a consumer 360 camera, which shows immediately in low light and in highlight roll-off through windows.
items.flop: Insta360's marketing pushed the X3 and everything after it, all of which use far smaller sensors but look sleeker and sell on viral social clips. The better-imaging model was quietly left behind.
items.catch: Not waterproof without the case. The exposed lenses scratch easily and guards are a separate purchase, so budget for them. Stitching workflow is slower than current models.
items.why: Business kit: fast scouting and rough-cut walkthroughs ahead of a proper bracketed DSLR shoot, without dragging the tripod round twice.

items.name: ASUS ProArt Studiobook / ProArt P16
items.spec: Calibrated OLED panel out of the box, discrete RTX graphics, full-size SD Express slot, and a physical control dial that maps to Adobe and video tools.
items.flop: ASUS spends its marketing on ROG gaming machines, and creative buyers default to a MacBook Pro without shopping around. ProArt sits in the middle with nobody advertising to it.
items.catch: Heavy, and the fans are audible under load. OLED panels on used units can carry burn-in from taskbars, so ask for a photo of a full-white screen. Resale is slow.
items.why: Keep. Colour-accurate panel plus a GPU is the combination you otherwise pay Apple a premium for.

items.name: Dell Precision 5570 / ThinkPad P1 Gen 5
items.spec: XPS-grade chassis with workstation graphics, 4K panel options, and support for 64GB of RAM and two NVMe drives. Certified drivers for CAD and 3D work.
items.flop: Corporate fleets dump these on three-year cycles. Private buyers do not know that "Precision" means an XPS with a professional GPU in it, so they scroll past and buy a consumer laptop for more money.
items.catch: Thermal throttling is real under sustained load, so check the fans spin freely. Batteries at this age are often at 60% health. Watch for BIOS supervisor passwords and active asset-management locks.
items.why: Flip, with a caveat: these move well to anyone doing 3D or CAD, and a RAM and SSD top-up from your donor stock lifts the sale price more than it costs.

items.name: Technics EAH-A800
items.spec: Around 50 hours of battery with noise cancelling on, LDAC support, and a genuinely good eight-microphone call setup that beats most of the big names on voice clarity.
items.flop: Technics is a Panasonic hi-fi brand nobody associates with headphones. It gets no shelf space next to Sony and Bose, so it competes on nothing but spec sheets that buyers never read.
items.catch: Build feels plastic for the price. The app is basic next to Sony's. Check the headband padding and the folding hinges, which are the usual failure points.
items.why: Flip. Low enough buy-in that even slow movement leaves margin, and counterfeits are not a problem because nobody bothers faking it.

items.name: Sennheiser Momentum 4 Wireless
items.spec: Around 60 hours of playback, which is roughly double the Sony equivalent, with the best plain sound quality in the price bracket and a proper parametric EQ in the app.
items.flop: Sennheiser's consumer arm changed hands and the marketing spend evaporated. The design is also deliberately plain, which kills it on a shop shelf against Sony and Bose.
items.catch: Noise cancelling is a step behind the Sony XM5. No folding hinge, so the case is bulky. Early units had a firmware fault that drained the battery in standby, so confirm it has been updated.
items.why: Flip. The audio crowd knows these, so there is a real buyer pool even if the general public does not.

items.name: LG gram 16 / 17
items.spec: A 17-inch screen at around 1.35kg, with an 80Wh battery. Nothing else puts that much screen in that little weight, and it still runs a full day unplugged.
items.flop: LG is a TV and appliance brand in most buyers' heads. It has no laptop presence in UK retail, so the gram sells almost entirely to people who already went looking for it.
items.catch: The chassis flexes, which is the price of the weight. Speakers are poor. Integrated graphics only, so no good for rendering. Check the hinges and the lid for stress cracks.
items.why: Keep. If you are carrying a machine round sites all day, the weight difference is the feature.

items.name: HONOR Magic7 Pro
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 5270mAh, and a 200MP periscope that is one of the better long-range phone cameras made. Sold officially in the UK, so it carries a real warranty and proper network support.
items.flop: Honor has had no brand equity in the UK since the Huawei split. It sells a flagship the equal of a Galaxy S25 and the public reads the badge as a budget brand, so it depreciates like one.
items.catch: Update commitment is shorter than Samsung's or Google's, so check what it is still receiving. MagicOS is heavy on duplicate apps. Check the curved screen edges for pressure marks.
items.why: Keep, and the best risk-adjusted phone on this list: UK stock, UK warranty, grey-import pricing without the grey-import problems.

items.name: Xiaomi 15 Ultra
items.spec: One-inch main sensor with Leica tuning, a 200MP periscope, Snapdragon 8 Elite and 5410mAh. In pure camera hardware terms it outguns anything Apple or Samsung shipped that year.
items.flop: Xiaomi sells officially in the UK but spends almost nothing on brand advertising here, and most buyers still file it under cheap. A £1,299 Xiaomi was always going to sit on shelves.
items.catch: The camera is only as good as the processing, and Xiaomi's has been inconsistent across updates. HyperOS ships with bloat. Confirm it is the global ROM and not a converted Chinese unit.
items.why: Keep. If you want a pocket camera that genuinely holds up for stills, this is the most camera per pound in the list.

items.name: Vivo X200 Pro / OPPO Find X8 Pro
items.spec: Dimensity 9400, 6000mAh and 5910mAh respectively, Zeiss and Hasselblad camera systems with genuinely excellent periscope telephotos. Both are top-tier hardware by any measure.
items.flop: Neither brand sells properly in the UK. With no retail presence, no carrier deals and no advertising, the only buyers are people who already knew what they wanted.
items.catch: This is the risky one. Grey import means no UK warranty and no local repair route. VoLTE and WiFi calling are frequently broken on UK networks, which means no calls on 4G or 5G. Confirm it is a global ROM with Play Services, not a Chinese ROM, and confirm VoLTE works on your network before money changes hands.
items.why: Keep, if and only if you verify VoLTE on your own SIM first. Fail that check and it is an expensive iPod.

items.name: Sony Xperia 1 VII
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 5000mAh, headphone jack, microSD, and the manual camera controls Sony keeps shipping while everyone else removes them. 4K OLED display.
items.flop: Same story as every Xperia: no UK carrier presence, no advertising, a price nobody would pay for a brand with no heat behind it. Sony sells these to people who hunt them down.
items.catch: Early units had a faulty circuit board causing random shutdowns, and Sony ran a replacement programme from July 2025. Dial *#06# for the IMEI and run it through Sony's own IMEI checker before you buy. If the seller will not give you the IMEI, walk.
items.why: Keep. Verify the IMEI first, then it is one of the best value flagships going.

items.name: OnePlus 13
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 6000mAh silicon-carbon battery, 100W wired charging, and a properly good display. Battery life was among the best in its year.
items.flop: OnePlus lost its enthusiast identity when it merged software with OPPO, and never built a mainstream one to replace it. It now sits in a gap: too expensive for bargain hunters, too obscure for flagship buyers.
items.catch: Silicon-carbon batteries are newer chemistry with less of a track record, and replacements are hard to source in the UK. Check charging behaviour at high percentages. No official UK carrier support.
items.why: Flip. The enthusiast pool still knows and wants OnePlus, so these actually move, unlike most of this list.

items.name: Galaxy S25 Edge
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 6.7in display, and an unusually thin body. On paper the discount looks like every other entry on this page.
items.flop: It did not flop for want of marketing. Samsung promoted it hard. It flopped because a 3900mAh battery in a 6.7in flagship means it runs out before the day does, and thinness turned out to be a feature nobody had asked for.
items.catch: The discount is the market pricing a real defect, not an oversight. Thin bodies also mean less room for heat, so sustained performance drops off. Resale will keep sliding.
items.why: Trap, and it is on this list as the control case. Before buying any steep discount, ask whether the thing was ignored or rejected. Ignored is a sleeper. Rejected is just a cheap bad product.

items.name: Lenovo ThinkCentre M720q / M920q Tiny
items.spec: A one-litre desktop with a proper quad or six-core desktop chip, two RAM slots, an NVMe slot and a 2.5in bay. Draws about 10W idle and is effectively silent.
items.flop: Office clearance stock with no consumer marketing behind it. People shopping for a small PC see a Raspberry Pi or a new NUC and never learn that a far more capable machine sells for the price of the Pi's case and PSU.
items.catch: Often sold with no power brick, which is a proprietary square tip, so check. Some are locked with a BIOS supervisor password. The 35W T-series chips are slower than the 65W ones for the same money, so read the exact model number.
items.why: Business kit at pocket-money prices. Two of these will run your n8n stack and a backup target with change from £200. Cheapest route off a VPS bill there is.

items.name: Sennheiser HD 560S / HD 599
items.spec: Genuinely neutral reference tuning, replaceable pads and cable, comfortable for hours. If you are cutting audio for client videos, these tell you what is actually in the file.
items.flop: Wired headphones with no noise cancelling and no brand heat. They are sold to a audio crowd that already knows about them and advertised to nobody else.
items.catch: Open-back, so everyone near you hears them and they leak in noise. No use on a train or a shoot. Check the headband for the known crack point where the slider meets the cup.
items.why: Keep. Buy for the editing desk, not for travel.

items.name: Reolink PoE cameras + NVR
items.spec: 4K or 5MP over a single ethernet run, records locally to the NVR or a NAS, works over RTSP with anything. No subscription, no cloud account required.
items.flop: Ring and Nest spend fortunes on advertising a monthly fee. Reolink sells hardware that needs no fee, which means no recurring revenue to fund advertising, which means nobody has heard of it.
items.catch: Running cable is the real cost, not the camera. The phone app is functional rather than polished. Check the firmware is current and the unit is not an older model that phones home to a region you do not want.
items.why: Keep. Covers your own premises and kit storage for a one-off cost instead of a direct debit.

items.name: TP-Link Omada EAP access points
items.spec: Ceiling or wall APs with PoE, proper VLAN and guest network support, and a free controller you can run on any machine, including one of those Tiny PCs.
items.flop: Ubiquiti owns the entire conversation about prosumer networking through sheer community presence. Omada does the same job for roughly half the money and has almost no mindshare outside installers.
items.catch: You need PoE, so budget for a PoE switch or injectors. Controller versions and hardware revisions have to match, so check the revision number on the label, not the listing title.
items.why: Flip, with decent margin. Small businesses and installers buy these, and the buyer pool knows what it is looking at.

items.name: Brother mono laser (HL-L2350DW class)
items.spec: Duplex mono laser, wireless, and toner that costs pence per page from third parties. Sits unused for months and still prints first time, which inkjets famously do not.
items.flop: HP and Epson spend their marketing on ink subscription models, because that is where the money is. A printer that costs almost nothing to run after purchase has nobody advertising it.
items.catch: Check the page count in the menu before buying and confirm the drum unit life remaining, which is separate from toner. Avoid units where a starter toner is the only one included.
items.why: Keep. Boring, and it will quietly save you more per year than most things on this list.

items.name: Zoom H1essential / Tascam DR-05X
items.spec: 32-bit float recording on the newer Zooms, which means a clipped take is recoverable in the edit. Runs off AA batteries, records to microSD, takes a lav via 3.5mm.
items.flop: Audio recorders are bought by a small professional crowd and advertised to nobody. Everyone else assumes the camera microphone will do, finds out it will not, and still never goes looking for one of these.
items.catch: Built-in mics are fine for room tone and poor for interviews, so budget for a lav. Check the 3.5mm jack for crackle by wiggling a plug in it. Older DR-05 models are not 32-bit float, which is the whole point.
items.why: Business kit. If you ever record a client talking about their venue for a walkthrough or a social clip, clean audio is what makes it look professional.

items.name: Panasonic Lumix G9 / GX9 (Micro Four Thirds)
items.spec: Weather-sealed body, excellent in-body stabilisation, and a high-resolution mode that composites a 80MP file from sensor shifts. Lenses are small, sharp and cheap because the whole system collapsed in price.
items.flop: The industry narrative decided full-frame had won and Micro Four Thirds was finished. Bodies and glass fell through the floor on sentiment rather than on performance.
items.catch: Smaller sensor, so low light is a real step behind full-frame. The format's future is genuinely uncertain, which caps resale. Check the shutter count and the rubber grips, which go sticky with age.
items.why: Keep. The stabilisation and the cheap sharp glass make it a strong second body for handheld interior work.

items.name: DJI Mic 2 / Mic Mini
items.spec: Two transmitters and a receiver in a charging case, 32-bit float internal recording on the Mic 2, and onboard backup recording so a dropout does not kill the take.
items.flop: This is not a marketing failure, it is an abandonment one. Bought for a YouTube channel that lasted four videos. Comes back to market boxed, barely used, with every clip and cable still bagged.
items.catch: Check all three units charge and pair, not just the receiver. The magnetic clips get lost first, so confirm they are present. Verify the case hinge and that the lid closes flush.
items.why: Flip. Creators are a steady buyer pool and these move reliably. The condition on abandoned kit means you can list it as near-new.

items.name: Elgato Stream Deck / Key Light / capture cards
items.spec: The Stream Deck is a programmable macro pad that runs anything you can script, not just streaming. Key Lights are properly colour-accurate panels controllable from the desktop.
items.flop: Pandemic-era streaming ambitions that did not survive contact with reality. Enormous volume of this stuff came to market when people went back to the office and stopped streaming.
items.catch: Capture cards date fast, so check the model supports the resolution you want. Stream Deck software is account-tied but the hardware is not locked. Key Light power bricks go missing.
items.why: Keep the Stream Deck. Mapped to your editing and stitching shortcuts it is a genuine time saver, and nothing else does that job for £50.

items.name: DJI Osmo Mobile 5 / 6 gimbal
items.spec: Three-axis phone stabiliser, folds flat, built-in extension rod on the later models. Turns a walked shot through a venue from unusable to smooth.
items.flop: Classic drawer gear. Bought for one holiday, used once, folded away. Volume on the used market is enormous and prices reflect it.
items.catch: Test all three motors hold under load with a phone fitted, not empty. The clamp arms crack. Check the folding joint is not loose. Missing counterweights and tripod feet are common.
items.why: Flip, cheaply and often. Low buy-in, steady demand, and they ship easily.

items.name: Huion Kamvas / XP-Pen Artist pen displays
items.spec: Screen you draw directly on, 8192 pressure levels, battery-free pen. The panels on the newer ones are laminated and colour-calibrated, which was a Wacom-only feature at four times the money.
items.flop: Two causes stacked: Wacom owns the brand conversation entirely, and these are a textbook new-hobby purchase that gets abandoned when the drawing habit does not stick.
items.catch: Pen nibs wear out and spares get lost, so check some are included. Test for parallax and dead pixels. The three-cable setup is fiddly and the breakout cable is proprietary, so it must be present.
items.why: Keep if you do any retouching or masking work. Far faster than a mouse for cutting people out of pano stitches.

items.name: Entry 3D printers (Ender 3 / Prusa Mini class)
items.spec: Usually sold with hundreds of pounds of upgrades already fitted by an owner who went deep for three months: better hotend, auto-levelling, upgraded board, spare nozzles, part-used filament.
items.flop: Highest abandonment rate of anything in consumer tech. The gap between buying a printer and reliably printing something useful defeats most people inside a season.
items.catch: Check the bed is not warped by looking down its length. Ask for a photo of a recent print, not a photo of the machine. Seized Z-rods and stripped extruder gears are the usual faults. Collection only, realistically.
items.why: Flip. The upgrades are free money because sellers almost never price them in, and the buyer pool knows exactly what those parts are worth.

items.name: Lenovo Legion Go
items.spec: An 8.8-inch 144Hz 1600p screen, Z1 Extreme chip, and detachable controllers. The biggest and sharpest display in the handheld class by a clear margin.
items.flop: It arrived beside the Steam Deck OLED, and Valve owned the conversation entirely. Windows handhelds also carry a reputation for software jank that put off the mainstream buyer.
items.catch: Battery life is poor at high settings. Windows handheld software is genuinely fiddly. Test both detachable controllers for stick drift and check the hall-effect sticks are the later revision.
items.why: Flip. Gaming handhelds still turn over faster than anything else on this list.
